content.text: I've read every source, draft section, numeral entry, figure brief, rendered sheet, and prior-art file. Here are my findings.

input.summary: The text is, on the whole, faithful to the inventor's disclosure and the five prior-art characterisations in the Background are all supported by the corresponding prior_art/ files (I checked each [REF:...] sentence against its source; none overstates what the file says). The specification is internally consistent in terminology (one name per element throughout), the 22-entry numeral table matches every numeral used in the text, and the claims are supported by the detailed description. The serious problems are in the drawings: on three of the five rendered sheets a leader dot lands on a different part from the one the numeral names (FIG. 3 numeral 24 lands inside the loop rather than on it; FIG. 4 numerals 34 and 38 land inside the covering-element hatching; FIG. 2 numeral 30 lands above the base in the bore of an unlabelled duct), FIG. 1 shows no covering element at all although the Brief Description and the detailed description both say it does, and FIG. 1 gives numerals 10 and 20 to the same block. On the text side, the second-embodiment "attachment formation" and its low placement / in-plane pull direction — which are recited in claims 15 and 19 — have no basis in input/disclosure.md, and a handful of variant embodiments (divided chambers, particulate separator, vertical-surface use) are additions the sources do not support.

findings.title: FIG. 4: numerals 34 (clearance) and 38 (exposed face) both land inside the covering-element hatching, and no clearance gap is drawn
findings.where: figures/rendered-FIG-4.png; figures/FIG-4-ENLARGED-FRAGMENTARY-SECTION-OF-THE-PERIMETER-MEMBE.md; draft/07-detailed-description.md (paragraph beginning "Because the perimeter member 24 is rigid…")
findings.detail: The detailed description makes FIG. 4 the one sheet that shows the clearance: "the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height." In the rendered sheet the foot of the column and the top of the first hatched band are separated only by a hairline sliver, and the leader dot carrying numeral 34 sits well to the right of the column (about x=1155), roughly 20 px BELOW the top edge of the first hatched band — i.e. inside the covering element 36, where no gap exists at all. The dot for numeral 38 likewise sits at mid-depth inside that same first band rather than on its top edge line. The result is that three numerals (34, 36 and 38) all point into one and the same hatched body, so the clearance and the exposed face are not distinguishable on the sheet. (The dot for 40 also appears to sit just below the second internal line, i.e. in the third band with 42 rather than in the second band; that one is close to the line and I am less certain of it.)
findings.evidence: Detailed description: "a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4 … the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height."  Figure brief: "The clearance 34 is the open white gap between the foot of the column and the top of the first band, drawn tall, so column and band nowhere touch. Identified in that gap toward its right." and "The exposed face 38 is the top edge of that first band, the line where the white gap above meets the hatching below."
findings.fix: Redraw FIG. 4 with the gap between the foot of the column and the top of the covering-element band opened to a clearly visible height, move the 34 endpoint into that white gap, and move the 38 endpoint onto the top boundary line of the first band; confirm 40 sits in the second band and 42 in the third.

findings.title: FIG. 3: numeral 24 points inside the loop instead of at the loop, and the sheet carries a fourth, undescribed rectangle
findings.where: figures/rendered-FIG-3.png; figures/FIG-3-BOTTOM-PLAN-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE.md; draft/06-drawings.md
findings.detail: The rendered bottom plan view contains four concentric rectangles plus the circle, not the three rectangles plus circle the brief specifies: the innermost outline is doubled by a second rectangle a few pixels inside it. Measuring the endpoint dots against those lines, the dot for 24 (right side, y≈405) lies about 30 px inboard of the innermost rectangle, i.e. in the area enclosed by the loop (the chamber side), not on the loop band between the second and third rectangles where the brief places it; the dot for 16 lies in the band between the second and third rectangles rather than in the outer margin between the first and second. So the numeral for the perimeter member does not sit on the perimeter member, and the extra rectangle corresponds to no part named in the specification. My pixel estimates carry some error, but under every reading of which rectangle is which, the 24 endpoint falls inboard of the innermost line and one rectangle is unaccounted for.
findings.evidence: Figure brief: "The sheet holds exactly four closed lines and nothing else … a large rectangle, a second rectangle within it, a third rectangle within that, and a circle within the third… No stroke is doubled by a close parallel line beside it" and "The perimeter member 24 is the surface between the second and third rectangles, the loop seen end on. Identified on the right run of that surface … halfway between the right line of the second rectangle and the right line of the third."  Detailed description: "In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a continuous closed loop … standing a little inboard of the outer edge of the base 12 so that a plain margin of the second side 16 lies outside the loop, as seen in the bottom plan view."
findings.fix: Regenerate FIG. 3 with exactly three single-stroke rectangles (base outline, loop outer edge, loop inner edge) plus the circle, and place the 24 endpoint at the mid-width of the loop band and the 16 endpoint in the margin between the base outline and the loop outer edge.

findings.title: FIG. 1 shows no covering element, although both the Brief Description and the detailed description say it does
findings.where: figures/rendered-FIG-1.png; draft/06-drawings.md; draft/07-detailed-description.md (Overview)
findings.detail: The rendered sheet contains a single flat slab, and the endpoint for numeral 12 (base) sits on that slab's upper surface; the motor block, the duct column and the handle bail all stand on the same slab. There is no second, larger slab beneath it, so no tile/covering element is shown, and neither bonding material nor substrate appears. The Brief Description nevertheless says the device is "shown resting on a covering element", and the Overview says FIG. 1 shows the device in use on a covering element laid on bonding material over a substrate. The sheet's own brief also calls for a tile that is absent from the render. (If instead the large slab is meant to be the tile, then numeral 12 is placed on the covering element rather than on the base — either way the sheet and the text disagree.)
findings.evidence: draft/06-drawings.md: "FIG. 1 is a perspective view of a vibration device according to a first embodiment, shown resting on a covering element."  draft/07-detailed-description.md: "FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 show a vibration device 10 in use. A covering element 36 … has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42."  Figure brief: "A large plain tile fills the lower sheet, larger than the device, with no joint line or second tile. - The base 12 is a flat rectangular slab lying on that tile…"
findings.fix: Either regenerate FIG. 1 with the tile beneath the base as the brief requires (keeping the 12 endpoint on the base), or amend the Brief Description and the Overview so that FIG. 1 is not said to show the device resting on a covering element bedded in bonding material over a substrate.

findings.title: FIG. 1: numerals 10 and 20 both terminate on the pump housing block
findings.where: figures/rendered-FIG-1.png; figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md
findings.detail: On the rendered sheet the dot for 10 sits on the front face of the upper block (about x=790, y=148) and the dot for 20 sits on the same block at its right-hand corner (about x=912, y=138), roughly 120 px apart on one body. Numeral 10 is defined as the whole assembly and was to be placed at the centre of that block's top face; as rendered, a reader cannot tell that 10 designates the assembly rather than the air-extraction mechanism, and the same body carries two numerals. review/previous-qa.md records the same defect ("Numeral 10 stayed within a rejected coordinate cluster … misplaced numerals 10"), which the current sheet does not appear to have cured.
findings.evidence: Figure brief: "The vibration device 10 is the whole assembly of slab, blocks, column, handle and cable, its highest surface the flat top face of the upper block. Identified at the centre of that top face, midway between its front and rear edges and midway between its left and right edges, on plain paper of the face, touching no edge, corner or other body." and "The air-extraction mechanism 20 … Identified on its flat right-hand face at mid-height, below that face."
findings.fix: Move the 10 endpoint onto the flat top face of the upper block (or, better, onto a part of the assembly not already carrying a numeral) so that 10 and 20 no longer share the same visible body.

findings.title: FIG. 2: numeral 30 lands above the base in the bore of an unlabelled duct, and 26 does not sit on the bearing-face line
findings.where: figures/rendered-FIG-2.png; figures/FIG-2-SIDE-ELEVATION-IN-VERTICAL-SECTION-SHOWING-THE-CHA.md; draft/07-detailed-description.md
findings.detail: The rendered section shows two hatched uprights standing above the slab and flanking the central channel — plainly the walls of the duct in section — although the sheet's own brief says the sheet shows "three hatched bodies and nothing else" and that "The equipment on top of the plate is omitted". The dot for numeral 30 sits between those uprights at about y=215, well above the slab's upper edge (y≈262), so the numeral for an opening the specification says "passes through the base 12" is placed in the bore of the (unnumbered) duct 32 rather than within the base thickness. Separately, the dot that appears to belong to numeral 26 sits at about (358, 610), at the inner edge of the left leg some 40 px above the line where the leg meets the covering-element band, rather than on that line as the brief directs; the 22 and 26 leaders converge closely there, and I am less certain which dot belongs to which numeral.
findings.evidence: Detailed description: "An extraction opening 30 passes through the base 12 from the second side 16 to the first side 14 and places the chamber 22 in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20 through a duct 32."  Figure brief: "The extraction opening 30 is the channel through the slab at the mid-width … Identified in that white paper at half its height, touching neither bounding line." and "The bearing face 26 is that common line where a leg meets the top edge of the band. Identified at one point on it beneath the left-hand leg."
findings.fix: Bring the 30 endpoint down into the channel within the thickness of the slab, and either delete the two uprights above the plate (as the brief states) or label them 32; move the 26 endpoint onto the leg/band contact line beneath the left-hand leg and separate it from the 22 leader.

findings.title: The attachment formation, its low placement and the in-plane direction of the pull are not in the inventor's disclosure, and are recited in claims 15 and 19
findings.where: draft/07-detailed-description.md ("Embodiment with a flexible pulling element"); draft/08-claims.md claims 15 and 19; figures/rendered-FIG-5.png
findings.detail: input/disclosure.md discloses only that a flexible pulling element is connected to the device and that pulling it moves the device while the pressure differential holds it down. The draft adds a named structure (attachment formation 48), a specific placement ("low on the base 12, close to the plane of the bearing face 26"), a stated mechanical consequence ("produces little moment tending to tilt the vibration device 10 about the leading edge of the perimeter member 24"), a direction limitation ("a pulling force substantially in the plane of the exposed face 38") and a further variant ("one at each end of the base 12, so that the vibration device 10 can be drawn in either direction"). None of these appears in the disclosure or in input/conversation.md. Two of them are claimed: claim 15 requires the pulling element to "apply to the vibration device a pulling force substantially in a plane of the exposed face", and claim 19 requires the attachment formation to be "positioned close to a plane of the bearing face so that tension … produces little moment tending to tilt the vibration device". The corresponding ring drawn low on the slab end is visible only on the generated FIG. 5 sheet.
findings.evidence: Disclosure: "In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface."  Draft: "In the embodiment of FIG. 5 the attachment formation 48 is placed low on the base 12, close to the plane of the bearing face 26, so that the line of the applied tension lies near that plane and produces little moment tending to tilt the vibration device 10 about the leading edge of the perimeter member 24."  Claim 19: "the attachment formation being positioned close to a plane of the bearing face so that tension applied to the flexible pulling element produces little moment tending to tilt the vibration device."
findings.fix: Either obtain the inventor's confirmation of the low attachment point and the in-plane pull, or cut the placement rationale and the anti-tilt statement from the description, delete claim 19, and amend claim 15 to recite only what the disclosure supports (a flexible pulling element connected to the device, position controlled by tension while the pressure differential supplies the holding force).

findings.title: Variant embodiments with no basis in the disclosure: divided chambers, particulate separator, vertical-surface use
findings.where: draft/07-detailed-description.md ("Further variations")
findings.detail: Three variations are described that the inventor's disclosure and the conversation do not mention at all: dividing the chamber into two or more chambers by rigid walls (together with asserted effects on pressure uniformity, base stiffness and added contact area), fitting a particulate separator in the duct, and use on walls or inclined surfaces with an accompanying friction/holding-force trade-off analysis. They are unclaimed and do not contradict the disclosure, but they are added embodiments and added results rather than explanation of disclosed material.
findings.evidence: Draft: "It may instead be divided into two or more chambers 22 by rigid walls standing on the second side 16 … Rigid walls used in this way also stiffen the base 12 against the alternating force from the vibration motor 18, and, standing on the second side 16 with their lower ends in the plane of the bearing face 26, they add further rigid contact area through which vibration passes into the covering element 36." and "A particulate separator may be fitted in the duct 32 …" and "For use on vertical surfaces the holding force is therefore raised, by increasing the plan area of the chamber 22 or the extraction rate of the air-extraction mechanism 20…". The disclosure says only: "The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials."
findings.fix: Confirm these variants with the inventor, or remove them (or reduce them to statements the disclosure supports) so the specification does not carry embodiments and effects the source does not.

findings.title: Summary asserts a comparative holding-force result the disclosure does not make
findings.where: draft/05-summary.md, third paragraph
findings.detail: The disclosure compares the invention's vibration transfer with that of a flexible suction cup, and says the operator need not press down; it nowhere states that the device is held against the tile more firmly than a pressed-on sliding base. The summary's "held down harder than a pressed-on sliding base" is a comparative performance result with no support in the source (the force an operator can apply to a sliding base is not discussed in magnitude anywhere in the disclosure).
findings.evidence: Summary: "The device is thus coupled harder and held down harder than a pressed-on sliding base, while the operator's hands carry less."  Disclosure: "A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer."
findings.fix: Reword to what the disclosure supports, e.g. that the holding force is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator and that the rigid path transmits vibration with less damping than a flexible suction cup.

findings.title: Absolute "no downward force" statements are stronger than the disclosure's "primarily for guiding"
findings.where: draft/07-detailed-description.md ("In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load."); draft/08-claims.md claim 23
findings.detail: The disclosure says the pressure differential holds the device "without requiring the operator to press downward" and that handles are "used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface" — wording that admits some incidental hand pressure. The description converts this into an absolute ("the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load"), and claim 23 recites it as a positive method limitation. Claims 6 and 18, which recite a holding force "sufficient to hold … without a downward force being applied by an operator", are capability statements and are fine; claim 23 is the one that asserts the operator in fact applies none.
findings.evidence: Disclosure: "The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface."  Claim 23: "…and wherein no downward force is applied to the vibration device by an operator while the vibration motor operates."
findings.fix: Soften the description sentence (e.g. "the operator need not carry any part of the contact load") and consider recasting claim 23's negative limitation as a capability, consistent with claims 6 and 18.

findings.title: FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 draw an unlabelled plate between the vibration motor and the base, against the text's "mounted directly against the first side"
findings.where: figures/rendered-FIG-1.png; figures/rendered-FIG-5.png; draft/07-detailed-description.md ("The vibration motor")
findings.detail: Both perspective sheets show the motor block standing on a separate thin plate that in turn stands on the base, with the fastener cubes on that plate. The single most emphasised structural point of the specification is that nothing at all is interposed between motor and base. The intervening plate is unlabelled and is not mentioned in either figure brief; it could be read as the motor's own foot flange, which is why I mark this minor, but as drawn it works against the text. FIG. 5 also carries a small unlabelled nozzle-like projection on the pump housing that its brief does not list ("The sheet contains only the parts listed").
findings.evidence: Detailed description: "It is mounted directly against the first side 14 and fixed to it by fasteners 54 spaced around its foot, as shown in FIG. 1, so that no resilient mount, rubber bush or foam pad is interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12."  Figure brief FIG. 1: "The vibration motor 18 is a rectangular block on the slab toward its left end, wider than tall, set back from the front edge."
findings.fix: Redraw the motor block seated directly on the base with the fastener heads on the base itself, and remove the unlisted projection from the pump housing in FIG. 5.

findings.title: FIG. 5: the 48 and 10 endpoints fall together near the cord and the slab corner rather than on the ring and the slab side face
findings.where: figures/rendered-FIG-5.png; figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-DEVICE-DRAWN-BY-A-FLEXIBLE-PULLI.md
findings.detail: On the rendered sheet the dot for 48 sits at roughly (865, 435) and the dot for 10 at roughly (900, 470) — both below and to the left of the ring, in the area where the cord leaves the ring and where the slab's lower left corner meets the floor. The brief requires 48 to sit on the ring's outline at the top of its opening and 10 to sit well inside the slab's near left side face, touching neither the cord nor the floor. My coordinate reading here has perhaps ±20 px of error, so I flag this as minor, but the two endpoints are visibly crowded together away from the surfaces the brief names.
findings.evidence: Figure brief: "The attachment formation 48 … Identified on that ring's outline at the top of the opening, level with the slab and clearly above the floor, and never on the floor, a joint line, the cord or the slab." and "The vibration device 10 … Identified within that side face, clearly above the floor and below the upper surface of the slab, and never on the floor, a joint line, the cord, the ring or either housing."
findings.fix: Re-place the 48 endpoint on the upper part of the ring's outline and the 10 endpoint at the centre of the slab's near left side face, separating the two leaders.

findings.title: Cross-reference section asserts "Not applicable" although the filing notes record priority status as unconfirmed, and no federally-sponsored-research statement is present
findings.where: draft/02-cross-reference.md; input/brief.md
findings.detail: input/brief.md records that priority status and government support status are both unconfirmed. The draft states "Not applicable" for the cross-reference, which is an affirmative representation the sources do not support, and there is no statement regarding federally sponsored research anywhere in the nine sections. I recognise the later instructions in input/conversation.md forbade leaving notes or placeholders for a person, so this is a conflict between the two sources rather than a drafting slip — but the file as it stands asserts a fact that has not been confirmed.
findings.evidence: draft/02-cross-reference.md: "Not applicable."  input/brief.md: "Priority status is not confirmed; leave a drafting note requesting it. Government support status is not confirmed; leave a drafting note requesting it."
findings.fix: Confirm priority and government-support status with the applicant before filing and set both statements accordingly, rather than leaving an unverified "Not applicable".

structured_output.summary: The text is, on the whole, faithful to the inventor's disclosure and the five prior-art characterisations in the Background are all supported by the corresponding prior_art/ files (I checked each [REF:...] sentence against its source; none overstates what the file says). The specification is internally consistent in terminology (one name per element throughout), the 22-entry numeral table matches every numeral used in the text, and the claims are supported by the detailed description. The serious problems are in the drawings: on three of the five rendered sheets a leader dot lands on a different part from the one the numeral names (FIG. 3 numeral 24 lands inside the loop rather than on it; FIG. 4 numerals 34 and 38 land inside the covering-element hatching; FIG. 2 numeral 30 lands above the base in the bore of an unlabelled duct), FIG. 1 shows no covering element at all although the Brief Description and the detailed description both say it does, and FIG. 1 gives numerals 10 and 20 to the same block. On the text side, the second-embodiment "attachment formation" and its low placement / in-plane pull direction — which are recited in claims 15 and 19 — have no basis in input/disclosure.md, and a handful of variant embodiments (divided chambers, particulate separator, vertical-surface use) are additions the sources do not support.

findings.title: FIG. 4: numerals 34 (clearance) and 38 (exposed face) both land inside the covering-element hatching, and no clearance gap is drawn
findings.where: figures/rendered-FIG-4.png; figures/FIG-4-ENLARGED-FRAGMENTARY-SECTION-OF-THE-PERIMETER-MEMBE.md; draft/07-detailed-description.md (paragraph beginning "Because the perimeter member 24 is rigid…")
findings.detail: The detailed description makes FIG. 4 the one sheet that shows the clearance: "the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height." In the rendered sheet the foot of the column and the top of the first hatched band are separated only by a hairline sliver, and the leader dot carrying numeral 34 sits well to the right of the column (about x=1155), roughly 20 px BELOW the top edge of the first hatched band — i.e. inside the covering element 36, where no gap exists at all. The dot for numeral 38 likewise sits at mid-depth inside that same first band rather than on its top edge line. The result is that three numerals (34, 36 and 38) all point into one and the same hatched body, so the clearance and the exposed face are not distinguishable on the sheet. (The dot for 40 also appears to sit just below the second internal line, i.e. in the third band with 42 rather than in the second band; that one is close to the line and I am less certain of it.)
findings.evidence: Detailed description: "a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4 … the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height."  Figure brief: "The clearance 34 is the open white gap between the foot of the column and the top of the first band, drawn tall, so column and band nowhere touch. Identified in that gap toward its right." and "The exposed face 38 is the top edge of that first band, the line where the white gap above meets the hatching below."
findings.fix: Redraw FIG. 4 with the gap between the foot of the column and the top of the covering-element band opened to a clearly visible height, move the 34 endpoint into that white gap, and move the 38 endpoint onto the top boundary line of the first band; confirm 40 sits in the second band and 42 in the third.

findings.title: FIG. 3: numeral 24 points inside the loop instead of at the loop, and the sheet carries a fourth, undescribed rectangle
findings.where: figures/rendered-FIG-3.png; figures/FIG-3-BOTTOM-PLAN-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE.md; draft/06-drawings.md
findings.detail: The rendered bottom plan view contains four concentric rectangles plus the circle, not the three rectangles plus circle the brief specifies: the innermost outline is doubled by a second rectangle a few pixels inside it. Measuring the endpoint dots against those lines, the dot for 24 (right side, y≈405) lies about 30 px inboard of the innermost rectangle, i.e. in the area enclosed by the loop (the chamber side), not on the loop band between the second and third rectangles where the brief places it; the dot for 16 lies in the band between the second and third rectangles rather than in the outer margin between the first and second. So the numeral for the perimeter member does not sit on the perimeter member, and the extra rectangle corresponds to no part named in the specification. My pixel estimates carry some error, but under every reading of which rectangle is which, the 24 endpoint falls inboard of the innermost line and one rectangle is unaccounted for.
findings.evidence: Figure brief: "The sheet holds exactly four closed lines and nothing else … a large rectangle, a second rectangle within it, a third rectangle within that, and a circle within the third… No stroke is doubled by a close parallel line beside it" and "The perimeter member 24 is the surface between the second and third rectangles, the loop seen end on. Identified on the right run of that surface … halfway between the right line of the second rectangle and the right line of the third."  Detailed description: "In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a continuous closed loop … standing a little inboard of the outer edge of the base 12 so that a plain margin of the second side 16 lies outside the loop, as seen in the bottom plan view."
findings.fix: Regenerate FIG. 3 with exactly three single-stroke rectangles (base outline, loop outer edge, loop inner edge) plus the circle, and place the 24 endpoint at the mid-width of the loop band and the 16 endpoint in the margin between the base outline and the loop outer edge.

findings.title: FIG. 1 shows no covering element, although both the Brief Description and the detailed description say it does
findings.where: figures/rendered-FIG-1.png; draft/06-drawings.md; draft/07-detailed-description.md (Overview)
findings.detail: The rendered sheet contains a single flat slab, and the endpoint for numeral 12 (base) sits on that slab's upper surface; the motor block, the duct column and the handle bail all stand on the same slab. There is no second, larger slab beneath it, so no tile/covering element is shown, and neither bonding material nor substrate appears. The Brief Description nevertheless says the device is "shown resting on a covering element", and the Overview says FIG. 1 shows the device in use on a covering element laid on bonding material over a substrate. The sheet's own brief also calls for a tile that is absent from the render. (If instead the large slab is meant to be the tile, then numeral 12 is placed on the covering element rather than on the base — either way the sheet and the text disagree.)
findings.evidence: draft/06-drawings.md: "FIG. 1 is a perspective view of a vibration device according to a first embodiment, shown resting on a covering element."  draft/07-detailed-description.md: "FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 show a vibration device 10 in use. A covering element 36 … has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42."  Figure brief: "A large plain tile fills the lower sheet, larger than the device, with no joint line or second tile. - The base 12 is a flat rectangular slab lying on that tile…"
findings.fix: Either regenerate FIG. 1 with the tile beneath the base as the brief requires (keeping the 12 endpoint on the base), or amend the Brief Description and the Overview so that FIG. 1 is not said to show the device resting on a covering element bedded in bonding material over a substrate.

findings.title: FIG. 1: numerals 10 and 20 both terminate on the pump housing block
findings.where: figures/rendered-FIG-1.png; figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md
findings.detail: On the rendered sheet the dot for 10 sits on the front face of the upper block (about x=790, y=148) and the dot for 20 sits on the same block at its right-hand corner (about x=912, y=138), roughly 120 px apart on one body. Numeral 10 is defined as the whole assembly and was to be placed at the centre of that block's top face; as rendered, a reader cannot tell that 10 designates the assembly rather than the air-extraction mechanism, and the same body carries two numerals. review/previous-qa.md records the same defect ("Numeral 10 stayed within a rejected coordinate cluster … misplaced numerals 10"), which the current sheet does not appear to have cured.
findings.evidence: Figure brief: "The vibration device 10 is the whole assembly of slab, blocks, column, handle and cable, its highest surface the flat top face of the upper block. Identified at the centre of that top face, midway between its front and rear edges and midway between its left and right edges, on plain paper of the face, touching no edge, corner or other body." and "The air-extraction mechanism 20 … Identified on its flat right-hand face at mid-height, below that face."
findings.fix: Move the 10 endpoint onto the flat top face of the upper block (or, better, onto a part of the assembly not already carrying a numeral) so that 10 and 20 no longer share the same visible body.

findings.title: FIG. 2: numeral 30 lands above the base in the bore of an unlabelled duct, and 26 does not sit on the bearing-face line
findings.where: figures/rendered-FIG-2.png; figures/FIG-2-SIDE-ELEVATION-IN-VERTICAL-SECTION-SHOWING-THE-CHA.md; draft/07-detailed-description.md
findings.detail: The rendered section shows two hatched uprights standing above the slab and flanking the central channel — plainly the walls of the duct in section — although the sheet's own brief says the sheet shows "three hatched bodies and nothing else" and that "The equipment on top of the plate is omitted". The dot for numeral 30 sits between those uprights at about y=215, well above the slab's upper edge (y≈262), so the numeral for an opening the specification says "passes through the base 12" is placed in the bore of the (unnumbered) duct 32 rather than within the base thickness. Separately, the dot that appears to belong to numeral 26 sits at about (358, 610), at the inner edge of the left leg some 40 px above the line where the leg meets the covering-element band, rather than on that line as the brief directs; the 22 and 26 leaders converge closely there, and I am less certain which dot belongs to which numeral.
findings.evidence: Detailed description: "An extraction opening 30 passes through the base 12 from the second side 16 to the first side 14 and places the chamber 22 in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20 through a duct 32."  Figure brief: "The extraction opening 30 is the channel through the slab at the mid-width … Identified in that white paper at half its height, touching neither bounding line." and "The bearing face 26 is that common line where a leg meets the top edge of the band. Identified at one point on it beneath the left-hand leg."
findings.fix: Bring the 30 endpoint down into the channel within the thickness of the slab, and either delete the two uprights above the plate (as the brief states) or label them 32; move the 26 endpoint onto the leg/band contact line beneath the left-hand leg and separate it from the 22 leader.

findings.title: The attachment formation, its low placement and the in-plane direction of the pull are not in the inventor's disclosure, and are recited in claims 15 and 19
findings.where: draft/07-detailed-description.md ("Embodiment with a flexible pulling element"); draft/08-claims.md claims 15 and 19; figures/rendered-FIG-5.png
findings.detail: input/disclosure.md discloses only that a flexible pulling element is connected to the device and that pulling it moves the device while the pressure differential holds it down. The draft adds a named structure (attachment formation 48), a specific placement ("low on the base 12, close to the plane of the bearing face 26"), a stated mechanical consequence ("produces little moment tending to tilt the vibration device 10 about the leading edge of the perimeter member 24"), a direction limitation ("a pulling force substantially in the plane of the exposed face 38") and a further variant ("one at each end of the base 12, so that the vibration device 10 can be drawn in either direction"). None of these appears in the disclosure or in input/conversation.md. Two of them are claimed: claim 15 requires the pulling element to "apply to the vibration device a pulling force substantially in a plane of the exposed face", and claim 19 requires the attachment formation to be "positioned close to a plane of the bearing face so that tension … produces little moment tending to tilt the vibration device". The corresponding ring drawn low on the slab end is visible only on the generated FIG. 5 sheet.
findings.evidence: Disclosure: "In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface."  Draft: "In the embodiment of FIG. 5 the attachment formation 48 is placed low on the base 12, close to the plane of the bearing face 26, so that the line of the applied tension lies near that plane and produces little moment tending to tilt the vibration device 10 about the leading edge of the perimeter member 24."  Claim 19: "the attachment formation being positioned close to a plane of the bearing face so that tension applied to the flexible pulling element produces little moment tending to tilt the vibration device."
findings.fix: Either obtain the inventor's confirmation of the low attachment point and the in-plane pull, or cut the placement rationale and the anti-tilt statement from the description, delete claim 19, and amend claim 15 to recite only what the disclosure supports (a flexible pulling element connected to the device, position controlled by tension while the pressure differential supplies the holding force).

findings.title: Variant embodiments with no basis in the disclosure: divided chambers, particulate separator, vertical-surface use
findings.where: draft/07-detailed-description.md ("Further variations")
findings.detail: Three variations are described that the inventor's disclosure and the conversation do not mention at all: dividing the chamber into two or more chambers by rigid walls (together with asserted effects on pressure uniformity, base stiffness and added contact area), fitting a particulate separator in the duct, and use on walls or inclined surfaces with an accompanying friction/holding-force trade-off analysis. They are unclaimed and do not contradict the disclosure, but they are added embodiments and added results rather than explanation of disclosed material.
findings.evidence: Draft: "It may instead be divided into two or more chambers 22 by rigid walls standing on the second side 16 … Rigid walls used in this way also stiffen the base 12 against the alternating force from the vibration motor 18, and, standing on the second side 16 with their lower ends in the plane of the bearing face 26, they add further rigid contact area through which vibration passes into the covering element 36." and "A particulate separator may be fitted in the duct 32 …" and "For use on vertical surfaces the holding force is therefore raised, by increasing the plan area of the chamber 22 or the extraction rate of the air-extraction mechanism 20…". The disclosure says only: "The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials."
findings.fix: Confirm these variants with the inventor, or remove them (or reduce them to statements the disclosure supports) so the specification does not carry embodiments and effects the source does not.

findings.title: Summary asserts a comparative holding-force result the disclosure does not make
findings.where: draft/05-summary.md, third paragraph
findings.detail: The disclosure compares the invention's vibration transfer with that of a flexible suction cup, and says the operator need not press down; it nowhere states that the device is held against the tile more firmly than a pressed-on sliding base. The summary's "held down harder than a pressed-on sliding base" is a comparative performance result with no support in the source (the force an operator can apply to a sliding base is not discussed in magnitude anywhere in the disclosure).
findings.evidence: Summary: "The device is thus coupled harder and held down harder than a pressed-on sliding base, while the operator's hands carry less."  Disclosure: "A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer."
findings.fix: Reword to what the disclosure supports, e.g. that the holding force is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator and that the rigid path transmits vibration with less damping than a flexible suction cup.

findings.title: Absolute "no downward force" statements are stronger than the disclosure's "primarily for guiding"
findings.where: draft/07-detailed-description.md ("In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load."); draft/08-claims.md claim 23
findings.detail: The disclosure says the pressure differential holds the device "without requiring the operator to press downward" and that handles are "used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface" — wording that admits some incidental hand pressure. The description converts this into an absolute ("the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load"), and claim 23 recites it as a positive method limitation. Claims 6 and 18, which recite a holding force "sufficient to hold … without a downward force being applied by an operator", are capability statements and are fine; claim 23 is the one that asserts the operator in fact applies none.
findings.evidence: Disclosure: "The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface."  Claim 23: "…and wherein no downward force is applied to the vibration device by an operator while the vibration motor operates."
findings.fix: Soften the description sentence (e.g. "the operator need not carry any part of the contact load") and consider recasting claim 23's negative limitation as a capability, consistent with claims 6 and 18.

findings.title: FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 draw an unlabelled plate between the vibration motor and the base, against the text's "mounted directly against the first side"
findings.where: figures/rendered-FIG-1.png; figures/rendered-FIG-5.png; draft/07-detailed-description.md ("The vibration motor")
findings.detail: Both perspective sheets show the motor block standing on a separate thin plate that in turn stands on the base, with the fastener cubes on that plate. The single most emphasised structural point of the specification is that nothing at all is interposed between motor and base. The intervening plate is unlabelled and is not mentioned in either figure brief; it could be read as the motor's own foot flange, which is why I mark this minor, but as drawn it works against the text. FIG. 5 also carries a small unlabelled nozzle-like projection on the pump housing that its brief does not list ("The sheet contains only the parts listed").
findings.evidence: Detailed description: "It is mounted directly against the first side 14 and fixed to it by fasteners 54 spaced around its foot, as shown in FIG. 1, so that no resilient mount, rubber bush or foam pad is interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12."  Figure brief FIG. 1: "The vibration motor 18 is a rectangular block on the slab toward its left end, wider than tall, set back from the front edge."
findings.fix: Redraw the motor block seated directly on the base with the fastener heads on the base itself, and remove the unlisted projection from the pump housing in FIG. 5.

findings.title: FIG. 5: the 48 and 10 endpoints fall together near the cord and the slab corner rather than on the ring and the slab side face
findings.where: figures/rendered-FIG-5.png; figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-DEVICE-DRAWN-BY-A-FLEXIBLE-PULLI.md
findings.detail: On the rendered sheet the dot for 48 sits at roughly (865, 435) and the dot for 10 at roughly (900, 470) — both below and to the left of the ring, in the area where the cord leaves the ring and where the slab's lower left corner meets the floor. The brief requires 48 to sit on the ring's outline at the top of its opening and 10 to sit well inside the slab's near left side face, touching neither the cord nor the floor. My coordinate reading here has perhaps ±20 px of error, so I flag this as minor, but the two endpoints are visibly crowded together away from the surfaces the brief names.
findings.evidence: Figure brief: "The attachment formation 48 … Identified on that ring's outline at the top of the opening, level with the slab and clearly above the floor, and never on the floor, a joint line, the cord or the slab." and "The vibration device 10 … Identified within that side face, clearly above the floor and below the upper surface of the slab, and never on the floor, a joint line, the cord, the ring or either housing."
findings.fix: Re-place the 48 endpoint on the upper part of the ring's outline and the 10 endpoint at the centre of the slab's near left side face, separating the two leaders.

findings.title: Cross-reference section asserts "Not applicable" although the filing notes record priority status as unconfirmed, and no federally-sponsored-research statement is present
findings.where: draft/02-cross-reference.md; input/brief.md
findings.detail: input/brief.md records that priority status and government support status are both unconfirmed. The draft states "Not applicable" for the cross-reference, which is an affirmative representation the sources do not support, and there is no statement regarding federally sponsored research anywhere in the nine sections. I recognise the later instructions in input/conversation.md forbade leaving notes or placeholders for a person, so this is a conflict between the two sources rather than a drafting slip — but the file as it stands asserts a fact that has not been confirmed.
findings.evidence: draft/02-cross-reference.md: "Not applicable."  input/brief.md: "Priority status is not confirmed; leave a drafting note requesting it. Government support status is not confirmed; leave a drafting note requesting it."
findings.fix: Confirm priority and government-support status with the applicant before filing and set both statements accordingly, rather than leaving an unverified "Not applicable".

5	The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.
6	
7	Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.
8	
9	Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.
10	
11	The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.
12	
13	Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.
14	
15	Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.
16	
17	The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

# Conversation so far

### USER

Here is my invention.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

1	The present disclosure relates to power tools for installing tiles and other covering elements, whether guided by hand or drawn across the work by a flexible pulling element, and more particularly to a vibration device that transmits mechanical vibration into a covering element that has been placed on a bed of thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material, in order to release trapped air, distribute the bonding material and improve the contact between the covering element and the bonding material.

file.content: The present disclosure relates to power tools for installing tiles and other covering elements, whether guided by hand or drawn across the work by a flexible pulling element, and more particularly to a vibration device that transmits mechanical vibration into a covering element that has been placed on a bed of thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material, in order to release trapped air, distribute the bonding material and improve the contact between the covering element and the bonding material.

content.content:
1	When a tile or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.
2	
3	Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place. In one known hand-held device for lifting and laying tiles, a handle carries two shafts, an electric motor vibrates the shafts, and a head shell at the free end of each shaft carries a suction cup on its underside, the suction cups being evacuated by an electrically operated pump and each being formed by a rubber-elastic apron [REF:DE-202021002652-U1].
4	
5	Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. A device gripped by such a cup is also anchored at one place on the covering element: it cannot be slid to another area without first releasing the grip, and the vibration amplitude reaching areas remote from the point of attachment falls off with distance from that point.
6	
7	Vacuum coupling arrangements used away from tile setting approach the holding of a body against a surface in other ways, each on the terms of its own document. In one adhesion device that holds itself to a wall surface, the peripheral wall of the decompressed space between the base and the wall surface is formed by elastic partitions, of which the partition nearer the wall surface has an end that contacts the wall surface, and a frame member of higher rigidity is added on the partition to restrict the partition from being deformed into that space as it is drawn down [REF:US-11408462-B2]. In a base assembly for coupling an end effector to a structure, a cavity on the second side of the assembly is held to the structure by vacuum drawn by a pneumatic generator operating in a suction mode, and the assembly is moved across the structure substantially frictionlessly on an air cushion produced by the same generator operating in a blower mode [REF:US-10001245-B2], so that the vacuum coupling is given up for the period during which the assembly is moved. In a device that suction-adheres to a wall surface and moves along it, a seal member mounted in the main body defines a pressure reduction space in cooperation with the wall surface, vacuum creating means discharges fluid from that space so that the main body adheres by the difference in fluid pressure inside and outside the space, and vibration generating means mounted on the main body imparts a lifting force in a direction away from the wall surface that reduces the suction-adhering force, together with a force along the wall surface that moves the main body [REF:US-4934475-A]. The vibration there is used to loosen the suction-adhering hold and to drive the main body along the wall surface. Vacuum is used differently again in handling equipment, where the object is to pick a workpiece up rather than to hold a tool down on it: in one vacuum plate lifting system for lifting sheet material articles, a substantially horizontal suction plate has a perforated suction lifting surface directed downward for contact with the upper surface of the article, an airflow suction system conveys vacuum air pressure to that surface, a lifter actuation system such as a robotic arm lifts and moves the plate, and an elongate bar movably mounted along an edge of the plate carries nozzles that are lowered to sweep a suction airflow across the surface beneath to remove dust or debris [REF:US-11247858-B2]. That system carries the article away from the work surface and cleans the work surface by suction; it does not deliver vibration into a covering element already laid on a bed of bonding material, and it accordingly says nothing about how a vibrating tool might be kept in contact with such a covering element while it is moved over it.
8	
9	The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile. Because contact has to be maintained by hand, the operator applies substantial and continuous downward force through the handle, and vibration travels back up that loaded path into the hands, wrists, arms and joints, producing discomfort, fatigue and a risk of injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles reduce some of the vibration reaching the operator, but they do so by absorbing mechanical energy that would otherwise have gone into the covering element, so the tool is made kinder to the operator by being made worse at its job. The two problems are coupled: firmer coupling to the covering element is obtained by pressing harder, and pressing harder is exactly what increases the vibration dose to the operator.
10	
11	What is needed is a way to hold a vibration device against a covering element with a force that does not come from the operator's arms, to conduct the vibration into the covering element without passing it through any compliant member, and to allow the device to be moved from area to area over the covering element without ever giving up that hold.
12

content.content:
1	A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side around the chamber and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials, and the bearing face is the end face of that member.
2
