In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 opposite the first side 14 and facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 at a perimeter of the second side 16, runs around the chamber 22, and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 is not compliant, and it transmits the vibration to the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than a flexible suction cup would.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, as seen in FIG. 2, and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

The perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air, where such a film remains, separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. Where a film of that kind remains beneath a sliding base of that kind, it lies between the base and the covering element over the whole area of the base, so that what crosses the interface crosses the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential. The handle 44 is shown schematically in FIG. 1.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and is supplied independently of the tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

content.content:
1	A vibration device for bedding covering elements into thinset, mortar or adhesive has a rigid base carrying a vibration motor and an air-extraction mechanism on its first side and a chamber on its second side. A rigid perimeter member of low-friction material such as plastic or PTFE surrounds the chamber, its end face forming a bearing face. It is not a seal: a clearance remains against the exposed face of the covering element, so ambient air enters the chamber continuously. Air is withdrawn fast enough to keep the chamber below atmospheric pressure while air keeps entering, and the pressure differential presses the device onto the covering element without downward force from the operator. Every member between the motor and the covering element is rigid, so vibration transfers with little damping, and the bearing face lets the device slide to successive areas without releasing the hold.

# FIG. 5 - Second embodiment with a pulling element

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, as FIG. 1. Outline line work only, with no lettering drawn. The vibration motor and the air-extraction mechanism are omitted.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile seen in perspective, as in FIG. 1, filling the lower part of the drawing area. The machine stands on its right-hand part, with open tile to the left.

The machine and the tile are shown schematically, the machine as one plain rectangular body standing on a band that runs round its underside, the band alone touching the tile, these forms being a convention for this sheet only.

The band meets the underside of the body and follows the same rectangular run, its front surface facing the viewer as one unbroken strip across the whole width and drawn deep, a broad clear surface standing between the underside of the body above and the tile below; its depth is schematic. It stands on the tile, its lower edge meeting the tile, and an open stretch of tile lies in front of the machine.

The rectangular body is drawn broad and tall, its front face turned toward the viewer as a large plain surface. Its right-hand end is one long straight edge between the top face and the band.

The flexible pulling element 46 is drawn as one slack curved path, in the manner of a loose cord. It begins where it meets the left-hand side of the machine, that meeting place shown schematically with no attachment formation, and runs away to the left, sagging over the open tile and stopping well inside the left-hand limit of the drawing area.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine standing on the covering element 36, the rectangular body with its band. Identified on the outer boundary line of the machine at the right-hand end of the rectangular body, anywhere along that long straight edge, clear of the flexible pulling element 46.
- The perimeter member 24 is the band under the rectangular body. Identified well inside the front strip of the band, above the line along which the band meets the tile and below the line along which it meets the body.
- The flexible pulling element 46 is that slack curved path. Identified on the path where it runs over the open tile, clear of the machine.
- The covering element 36 is that large plain tile, on which the machine stands. Identified well inside the open stretch of tile in front of the machine, clear of the flexible pulling element 46.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 10, 24, 36, 46

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10
- 24

- 46

Only one defect is reported, a modality overstatement in the detailed description that also conflicts with the draft's own Background.
4	
5	## Reviewer findings
6	
7	- **[minor] Detailed description states the prior-art air film as a certainty where the Background and the disclosure state it as a possibility** (draft/08-detailed-description.md, paragraph beginning "The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26..." (line ) - The Background hedges the prior-art sliding-base air film exactly as the inventor did: "even under that pressure a thin film of air CAN remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface" (draft/05-background.md line 5), tracking the disclosure's "even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile MAY dampen vibration transfer" (input/disclosure.md line 7). The detailed description then restates the same prior-art arrangement in absolute terms: the base "is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface MUST cross the film." The inventor's disclosure nowhere asserts that a pressed-on sliding base is in fact separated from the tile over its whole area; it says only that a layer of air may remain. The result is both an unsupported absolute about the prior art and an internal inconsistency of modality between two sections of the same application describing the same thing. The trailing clause of the same sentence keeps the correct hedge ("the film MAY dampen the vibration crossing it"), which makes the mismatch visible within a single sentence. I am marking this minor because the surrounding contrast the paragraph is drawing (rigid loaded contact versus an intervening film) is itself supported, and only the strength of the assertion is off.
8	  - Suggested fix: In draft/08-detailed-description.md line 51, replace "A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it." with "Where a film of that kind remains beneath a sliding base of that kind, it lies between the base and the covering element over the whole area of the base, so that what crosses the interface crosses the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it." This keeps the contrast the paragraph is making while restoring the disclosure's and the Background's hedged modality.
9

11	the wording or figure specification unambiguous enough that the check passes.

(line ) - The Background hedges the prior-art sliding-base air film exactly as the inventor did: "even under that pressure a thin film of air CAN remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface" (draft/05-background.md line 5), tracking the disclosure's "even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile MAY dampen vibration transfer" (input/disclosure.md line 7). The detailed description then restates the same prior-art arrangement in absolute terms: the base "is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface MUST cross the film." The inventor's disclosure nowhere asserts that a pressed-on sliding base is in fact separated from the tile over its whole area; it says only that a layer of air may remain. The result is both an unsupported absolute about the prior art and an internal inconsistency of modality between two sections of the same application describing the same thing. The trailing clause of the same sentence keeps the correct hedge ("the film MAY dampen the vibration crossing it"), which makes the mismatch visible within a single sentence. I am marking this minor because the surrounding contrast the paragraph is drawing (rigid loaded contact versus an intervening film) is itself supported, and only the strength of the assertion is off.
  - Suggested fix: In draft/08-detailed-description.md line 51, replace "A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it." with "Where a film of that kind remains beneath a sliding base of that kind, it lies between the base and the covering element over the whole area of the base, so that what crosses the interface crosses the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it." This keeps the contrast the paragraph is making while restoring the disclosure's and the Background's hedged modality.

content.text: I've read the disclosure and conversation, all ten draft sections plus numerals.md, all five figure briefs, all five rendered PNGs (hash-verified against the audit file), the audit evidence, and all five prior-art files.

input.summary: I traced every claim limitation, every one of the sixteen numbered parts, and every structure, material, relationship and result presented as part of the invention back to an exact passage in input/disclosure.md, and found no added core structure, embodiment, measurement or experimental fact. The features the user's corrective message flagged for deletion (separate PTFE facing, through-base opening/duct, support column, motor fasteners, exhaust to atmosphere, no-valve limitation, cord/battery, integral one-piece loop, attachment formation, plural chambers, vertical-surface use, bail-handle geometry) are absent from the text, the briefs and the sheets; the fluid-communication route is deliberately left unstated in both text and FIG. 2 brief, which is the source-faithful choice. All five rendered PNGs hash-match review/figure-audit-evidence.json; I opened each and confirmed that every printed numeral's leader terminates on the part its brief and numerals.md assign it, that no numeral labels two parts across sheets, and that nothing the Brief Description or detailed description says a figure shows is missing (FIG. 2 legs standing on the band with the clearance reserved to FIG. 4; FIG. 3 closed ring; FIG. 4 column, gap and three layers; FIG. 5 body, band and slack pulling element). The handle in FIG. 1 is a plain block, but the brief expressly disclaims form and mounting and the claims and description stay neutral, so I treat it as a generic depiction convention rather than a defect. All four [REF:...] characterisations are supported by the abstract or claim text in the corresponding prior_art/ file, including the negative statement about US-11247858-B2. Claim set is 18 claims / 3 independent, antecedent basis holds, terminology is one-name-per-element between claims and description, and the abstract is a single paragraph of about 144 words. Two notes that are not draft defects: the FIG. 3 endpoints.summary in the evidence file narrates a failure for numeral 24 that contradicts its own per-label correct:true verdict — I re-opened rendered-FIG-3.png and the dot sits roughly mid-band between the outer and inner ring edges, so the per-label verdict is right and the prose is stale; and pixel tooling was unavailable in this sandbox, so FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 hatch directions rest on the byte-exact section-hatch certificates, which record exact_renderer_match true against rendered-sheet hashes I verified by sha256. Only two minor internal-coherence items are reported.

findings.title: Background refers to "The second problem" but never identifies a first problem
findings.where: draft/05-background.md, paragraph beginning "The second problem with existing tile vibration devices..." (line 9), read against the paragraph beginning "Both arrangements couple the vibration..." (line 5)
findings.detail: The inventor's disclosure frames the prior-art shortcomings explicitly as a numbered pair: "Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile... Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure" (input/disclosure.md line 7-9). The Background keeps the second half of that framing but drops the first: the coupling problem is introduced only as "Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly", and an entire intervening paragraph about unrelated vacuum-coupling art ([REF:US-11408462-B2], [REF:US-10001245-B2], [REF:US-4934475-A], [REF:US-11247858-B2]) then separates it from the sentence that calls the operator issue "The second problem". The ordinal therefore has no antecedent in the document: no passage anywhere in the application identifies a first problem. This is a coherence gap only - the substance of both problems is present and faithful to the disclosure - so I mark it minor.
findings.evidence: draft/05-background.md line 5: "Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly." draft/05-background.md line 9: "The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile." input/disclosure.md line 7: "Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile."
findings.fix: In draft/05-background.md line 5, replace the opening sentence "Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly." with "The first of two problems with existing tile vibration devices is that both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly." This restores the inventor's own "two main disadvantages / First ... Second" framing and gives the later "The second problem" its antecedent, without adding any matter.

findings.title: Unnumbered "the base" in the detailed description denotes a prior-art sliding base, colliding with the claimed base 12
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md, second sentence of the paragraph beginning "The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26..." (line 51)
findings.detail: Throughout the application "base" is the claimed rigid element and is always written "the base 12" (e.g. line 7 "The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12...", line 47 "passes into the base 12 at the first side 14"). In this one sentence the same bare noun is used twice for a different, prior-art object - the pressed-on sliding base of the conventional tool described in the Background ("A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator", draft/05-background.md line 5). The antecedent "a sliding base of that kind" is present earlier in the same sentence, so the meaning is recoverable, but the application otherwise observes one-name-per-thing strictly, and reading "the base and the covering element" alongside "the base 12" and "the covering element 36" invites momentary confusion between the claimed element and the prior-art one. The same sentence also uses "the covering element" without its numeral for a hypothetical prior-art workpiece. I mark this minor because no technical statement is wrong and the fix is purely lexical.
findings.evidence: draft/08-detailed-description.md line 51: "Where a film of that kind remains beneath a sliding base of that kind, it lies between the base and the covering element over the whole area of the base, so that what crosses the interface crosses the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it."
findings.fix: In draft/08-detailed-description.md line 51, replace "it lies between the base and the covering element over the whole area of the base" with "it lies between that sliding base and the covering element beneath it over the whole area of that sliding base". This keeps the hedged modality and the contrast the paragraph draws, and reserves the bare term "base" for the claimed base 12.
